title: Sax models: Leonard Fields, Boyd Senter and a refined saxophone sound
summary: Carter discusses saxophonists he heard, and denies setting out to create a more refined alto style.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Okay. Now was the sound -- a couple of things interest me here; I'm not just merely being biographical, I hope, but I'm wondering about the quality of sound and the kind of artistry that these teachers may have encouraged you to develop, and this attention^to -- for lack of a better word, we might call 'legitimate' technique and exercises exercises and so forth -- was this of any great value to you then? Was it something that you really tried to apply to another idiom; a jazz idiom or a popular idiom -- or was it particularly unusual that people who were playing in a popular idiom would have had this kind of training?
See, I don't know quite how to answer that, because^I I don't know, I guess I have the sound in my head, or the sound that I wanted to get, you know?

And I don't know how to answer that ... there was a player around dude on at the time that I must mention, but I don't know that I've heard his name mentioned recently; oh, in many years, and a lot of people would probably not have considered him a jazz saxophonist, and his name was Leonard Fields; I think he was from Lexington, or maybe Louisville, Kentucky - and if things had been a little different for the
black musician at that time, he would have been the black Wiedoeft Rudy Weedoff, you know.

I don't think he ever did. He was a fantastic technician; absolutely fantastic, believe me. And he was much more jazz oriented than you know, than Rudy Wiedoeft, although he certainly wouldn't have been considered as jazz oriented as somebody like Johnny Hodges or Hilton Jefferson or Happy Haddie Caldwell, anybody like that.
What about a Boyd Centa? I mean he made a great number of records.

I heard a lot of records by Boyd Centa, and he probably made more records than anybody at that time -- I heard him all over the place, you know? But I was not particularly interested in sounding like, you know, he sounded. He had a good sound, as I remember, and I guess what he was doing, somebody considered it jazz. You know? And you know how I feel about the term, so I won't go in to that!
Jazzy, yeah, yeah. Maybe, you know. But yes, Boyd Centa was all over.
There's one thing maybe I can get your reaction to, and that is that in his book, "Jazz -- It's Evolution and Essence", Andre Hodler makes quite a

point that you were one ... now I don't want to overstate this, but one of, perhaps we would call it, a vanguard of younger musicians in the twenties, who -- with a certain kind of instrumental sound, a certain attention to what you might call a more delicate, more refined, or elegant style of playing, an attention to perhaps a more legitimate kind of articulation and vibrato and so forth, offered, as he describes a reaction to, and I think that I'm quoting him -- what he calls the "violently colored sonority of jazz music" of that time.
Did you see yourself as doing something which was particularly different in terms of the approach to the saxophone at this time?

No. I don't think a young musician usually thinks of seeing himself as doing something different. I think at that stage, if I'm thinking of the same stage or criteria you know, as you are eluding to, I believe, you're thinking of emulating someone who you hear; you're not really thinking in terms yet of, you know, innovations and creating something. Maybe somebody did. I certainly can't speak for a whole slew of young musicians, but at the time, I didn't; I wanted to sound like, I guess, Frankie Trumbauer, you know.
